8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":2,"verseId":3,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Motion","totalVerses":25,"verseData":{"id":"v2_3","number":3,"title":"Motion Cannot Inhere in the Mover","sanskrit":{"text":"gamyamānasya gamanaṃ katham nāmopapatsyate | gamyamānaṃ vigamanaṃ yadā naivopapadyate ||","transliteration":"gamyamānasya gamanaṃ katham nāmopapatsyate | gamyamānaṃ vigamanaṃ yadā naivopapadyate","translation":"How would it be acceptable For motion to be in the mover? When it is not moving, it is not acceptable To call it a mover."},"philosophy":{"insight":"Nāgārjuna now dismantles the opponent's v.2 claim. If motion were an inherent property of \"the mover,\" then the mover should always move — but movers can be stationary. The designation \"mover\" depends on the context of moving.","madhyamaka":"Garfield: this verse establishes that \"mover\" is a context-dependent designation, not an inherent nature. If motion were intrinsic to the mover, the mover could never rest. Kalupahana: the verse targets the reification of the agent-subject — the Sarvāstivādins treated the \"mover\" (gantṛ) as an inherently existing dharma, but Nāgārjuna shows the label is purely relational. Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā commentary reinforces: \"mover\" is an upādāya prajñapti (dependent designation).","quantum":"Kochen-Specker Theorem / Quantum Contextuality: Properties like spin direction do not exist independently of the measurement context. A particle doesn't \"have\" spin-up as an inherent property — it manifests spin-up only relative to a chosen measurement axis.","bridge":"Both show properties are context-dependent, not inherent. \"Mover\" is a designation that depends on the context of motion, just as \"spin-up\" is a value that depends on the measurement basis. Neither is an intrinsic, context-free property.","accessible":"Is a towel \"wet\"? Only when it has water on it. A dry towel isn't inherently \"wet\" — the wetness depends on context. Similarly, something is a \"mover\" only in the context of moving. When it stops, calling it a \"mover\" makes no sense. The label depends on the situation, not on some inner essence.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, we designate \"movers\" and \"motion\" without problem. Ultimately, the mover-designation depends on motion and vice versa — neither has independent ground.","commonMisconception":"This doesn't mean we can't call anyone a \"walker.\" We can — conventionally. The point is that \"walker\" isn't an INHERENT property; it's a dependent designation."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Kochen-Specker Theorem (Contextuality)","score":89,"strength":"High","explanation":"Properties emerge only relative to measurement context, not as inherent attributes. Both deny context-independent properties."},"animation":{"geometry":"Context-Switching Sphere","anchor":"A central sphere that switches between \"moving\" (with velocity trails) and \"stationary\" (solid, no trails) states. If motion were an inherent, inseparable property (like roundness of a sphere), the mover could never be stationary without ceasing to exist. Since movers obviously rest, motion isn't an inherent property.","realLifeExample":"A car can be parked. If \"moving\" were an inherent property of the car (like its colour), it could never stop. But it does — so \"moving\" is a state, not an essence."},{"q":"Is a \"mover\" not a real thing then?","a":"A \"mover\" exists conventionally — as a dependent designation. The label applies when something is moving and doesn't apply when it's still. When the course ends, you're not a \"student\" anymore (for that course). Change the axis and the value changes. The property doesn't pre-exist the context — just as \"mover\" doesn't pre-exist the motion.","realLifeExample":"Are you \"tall\"? Compared to a child, yes. Remove any of these and the contract ceases to function.
